renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Read length N50 per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the N50 of its read lengths, the length such that half of the sequenced bases sit in reads at least that long. It answers which libraries gave the longest reads for the sequenced yield.
    How to read: a taller bar means longer reads, which resolve repeats and structural variants better. Compare libraries prepared the same way, since a fragmentation or size selection step moves the N50 as much as the run does. Open the length against quality view to see whether a long library is also accurate.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median read length N50 of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of NanoStat.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wdecoster/nanomath/master/nanomath/nanomath.py
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: read_length_n50
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Library
      read_length_n50: Read length N50 (bases)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: read_length_n50

- component: card
  title: Total reads
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of reads over every library in view, and the bars rank the libraries that contribute most. It answers how much sequence the run produced and where it came from.
    How to read: a library far below its peers is under-loaded or failed early. Reads are not bases, so read this next to the yield card.
  column: n_reads
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: sample
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: the libraries with most reads

- component: card
  title: Total yield (Gb)
  description: |-
    The hero number is the sequenced yield in gigabases over every library in view, and the bars rank the libraries by yield. It answers whether the run produced enough data for the planned analysis.
    How to read: compare each library with the yield you planned for. NanoStat sets no minimum yield, so judge it against the experiment, not a fixed number.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  column: total_gigabases
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: sample
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: the libraries with most yield
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Read length N50
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median N50 across libraries, and the box shows how the libraries spread around it. It answers how long the reads are in a typical library and how consistent the libraries are.
    How to read: a tight box means the libraries were prepared alike. A wide box or a far outlier points to a library with a different size distribution, so open the table to find it.
  column: read_length_n50
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Mean read quality
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean of the libraries' mean read quality, a Phred score averaged over each read's bases, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers how accurate the basecalls are overall.
    How to read: higher is better and the value depends on the pore chemistry and the basecaller model, so compare libraries of one run. A library well below its peers deserves a look at the quality ladder tab before analysis.
  column: mean_read_quality
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: mean, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Mean read length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean of the libraries' mean read length in bases, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers how long a read is on average.
    How to read: the mean is pulled up by a few very long reads, so it sits above the median in a typical Nanopore library. A large gap between the two cards means a long tail.
  column: mean_read_length
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: mean, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Median read length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median of the libraries' median read length in bases, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers how long the middle read is, which a few very long reads do not move.
    How to read: compare it with the mean and the N50. A median far below the N50 means most reads are short while the bases sit in a few long ones.
  column: median_read_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Read length spread
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean standard deviation of read length, in bases, over the libraries, and the box shows how it varies between them. It answers how uneven the read lengths are.
    How to read: a large value relative to the mean length means a broad distribution, typical of unsheared or transposase library preparations. A tight value points to a size-selected library.
  column: stdev_read_length
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: mean, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Longest read
  description: |-
    The hero number is the longest read in any library in view, in bases, and the bars rank the libraries by their own longest read. It answers how far the length tail reaches.
    How to read: one extreme read says little on its own, since a single chimeric or concatenated read can dominate it. Read it with the N50.
  column: longest_read_length
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: sample
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: the libraries with the longest read

- component: card
  title: Median read quality
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median of the libraries' median read quality, a Phred score, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers what quality the typical read has.
    How to read: the median sits above the mean when a tail of poor reads drags the mean down. A library whose median is low as well has poor basecalls overall.
  column: median_read_quality
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: advanced_viz
  id: length_vs_quality
  title: Read length against quality
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: its mean read length on the horizontal axis, its mean read quality on the vertical axis, with the marker sized by sequenced yield. It answers whether the longest libraries are also the most accurate.
    How to read: libraries in the upper right give long and accurate reads. A library that is long but low in quality, or accurate but short, shows the trade-off of its preparation; with few libraries the points are best read next to the table. No pass mark is drawn because NanoStat defines none.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mean read quality of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of NanoStat.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Mean read length (bases)
    y_title: Mean read quality (Phred)
    legend_pos: bottom
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
  roles:
    x: mean_read_length
    y: mean_read_quality
    label: sample
    size: total_gigabases
    color: sample

- component: table
  title: Long-read summary table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with its NanoStat summary: read count, yield, read length mean, median, N50 and standard deviation, read quality and the longest read. It answers which library to inspect or exclude.
    How to read: sort by N50, quality or yield to find the weakest library, and compare the mean with the median to spot a long tail.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: quality_ladder
  title: Reads kept at each quality cutoff
  description: |-
    Each line is a library: the percentage of its reads whose mean quality is above each cutoff of the NanoStat ladder. It answers how fast a library loses reads as the quality floor rises.
    How to read: a line that stays high and drops late is a library tight around a good quality. A line that falls early is poor, and a steep drop between two rungs means a bimodal library that a single mean quality hides. Pick the cutoff for filtering from the rung where the curve starts to fall.
    Lines and annotations: no pass mark is drawn, because NanoStat defines none. The rungs are the fixed cutoffs of the NanoStat report.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Quality cutoff (Phred Q)
    y_title: Reads above the cutoff (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: q_cutoff
    y: pct_reads

- component: figure
  title: Yield above each quality cutoff
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library at one cutoff: the megabases carried by reads above that quality. It answers how much usable sequence remains after filtering at each rung.
    How to read: compare bars within a cutoff to rank libraries by usable yield. A library with a large yield at Q5 but a small one at Q10 is mostly low-quality sequence.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: q_cutoff
    y: megabases
    color: sample
    barmode: group
    labels:
      q_cutoff: Quality cutoff (Phred Q)
      megabases: Yield above the cutoff (Mb)
      sample: Library

- component: card
  title: Reads above Q10
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean percentage of reads above quality Q10 over the libraries, and the box shows the spread between them. It answers what share of reads survive a common basecall quality floor.
    How to read: a high value with a tight box means consistent libraries. Q10 is one rung of the ladder NanoStat reports and not a pass mark, so open the ladder line chart to see other rungs.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  column: pct_reads
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  filter_expr: col('q_cutoff') == 10
  caption: mean, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Yield above Q10 (Mb)
  description: |-
    The hero number is the megabases carried by reads above Q10 over every library in view, and the bars rank the libraries by it. It answers how much sequence is left after filtering at that quality.
    How to read: the ladder is cumulative, so a single rung is read, not a sum across rungs. A library that leads on total yield but not here has lower accuracy.
  column: megabases
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: sample
  top_n_count: 3
  filter_expr: col('q_cutoff') == 10
  caption: the libraries with most yield above Q10

- component: card
  title: Reads above Q10
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of reads above Q10 over every library in view, and the bars rank the libraries by it. It answers how many reads pass that quality floor.
    How to read: compare it with the total read count of the summary tab. A large loss means many low-quality reads.
  column: n_reads
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: sample
  top_n_count: 3
  filter_expr: col('q_cutoff') == 10
  caption: the libraries with most reads above Q10

- component: table
  title: Quality ladder table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library at one quality cutoff: reads, percentage of reads and megabases above it. It answers the exact numbers behind the ladder tiles.
    How to read: filter on one cutoff to compare libraries, or on one library to see its whole ladder.
